summary:
Karabük province stands under the national framework of the Republic of Turkey, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. As of 29 October 2025 a leaked omnibus measure known as the 11th Judicial Package was before the government. It would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' imprisonment, and would punish participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years' imprisonment; trans people receiving care deemed illegal would face up to three years. Human Rights Watch warns the package would drive treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention.

Checkpoint contact is the routine point of exposure for a visitor. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for GBT background checks before release. Any such interaction places a document in front of an officer whose details can be compared against presentation.

Lethal violence is documented at national level. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of them classified by rights organisations as hate killings, and transgender people were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, an asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

No Karabük-specific incident appears in the sources. The province is governed by the same national laws, ministries and police practice described here.
tangentialFactors:
Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring review records roughly 313 violations overall, about 2.5 times the previous year's total, alongside 299 detention decisions. Freedom-of-expression violations rose from 216 to 540 in the same period.

Hostility has been converted into administrative instruction. Public institutions received "Year of the Family" directives, an LGBTI+ association was closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members, and artistic events were cancelled or banned.

Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft package, and Human Rights Watch states that healthcare professionals and patients alike would be exposed to prosecution if it is enacted in its reported form.

Transition-related care is tightening through regulation rather than legislation. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Kaos GL records 89 torture and ill-treatment violations in 2025, up from 51 the prior year, and 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected.
outOfScopeNotes:
The draft package had not been passed when reported on 29 October 2025. Its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force: one of the women detained in Istanbul in 2025 stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was being applied to them.

The sources are national-framework reporting with no provincial breakdown. No Karabük-specific enforcement action, facility, detention or incident is sourced, and none is asserted here.

Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that GBT checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. That argument is unresolved in the sources; no court ruling on its validity is provided.

The September 2025 Health Ministry regulation is reported through secondary coverage and its full text is not reproduced in the inventory. Online framing of the change as an "LGBT opening" is contested, and the scope of the restriction on transition care is not independently verified here.
